name: English
intro: Use this volume from basic English upward: repair foundations, then study precision, register, argument and pronunciation. Advanced English is accurate and adaptable; an uncommon word used imprecisely weakens a sentence. The pronunciation models are contemporary standard southern British English and General American. Both have considerable internal variation. IPA between slashes is a broad pronunciation guide, not a recording of every possible speaker.

foundation.name: English
notes: Use the alphabet as a reference

You already read English. Keep this table for spelling aloud and move into the advanced grammar section. Letter names do not reliably predict pronunciation in words. English has many more vowel sounds than vowel letters.

Learn a word’s IPA, stressed syllable and recording together: record as a noun and record as a verb commonly differ in stress. schwa /ə/ is a frequent unstressed vowel. Connected speech changes the surface form while the written words remain the same.

The course contrasts contemporary standard southern British English and General American. General American is usually rhotic: /r/ in car. The southern British model usually drops post-vocalic /r/ before a pause/consonant. UK and US each contain many other accents. Listen to both model recordings and shadow phrases, not isolated letters.
building: analyse/analyze → analysis → analytical. Word class, spelling and stress can change. un- reverses many adjectives; re- often means again; neither works freely with every word.
make a decision, reach a conclusion, conduct research, strong evidence. A synonym does not automatically fit the same collocations. Research and evidence are normally uncountable in academic use.
The team revised the report. is clearer than The implementation of a revision was undertaken. Use nominalisation when it helps compare concepts, not to make every sentence longer.
phrases: Could you clarify what you mean?
Ask for a more precise explanation.
The evidence suggests a possible association.
State a cautious finding without claiming causation.
I agree with the aim, but I have concerns about the method.
Disagree with one specific aspect politely.
Would you mind repeating the last point?

sections.title: Foundation repair: the noun phrase
sections.explanation:
English articles encode how a reader identifies a referent. Use a/an for a singular countable noun introduced as one member of a class, the for a sufficiently identifiable referent, and zero article for many general plural and uncountable expressions. Identifiability can come from context, not just previous mention. A hospital can be one unspecified institution; the hospital can be the locally relevant one. British in hospital and American in the hospital also illustrate conventional regional usage.
Countability belongs to a word's meaning in context. Research and evidence are normally uncountable in general academic English: some evidence, a piece of evidence, several studies. Experience can be uncountable knowledge or a countable event. Generic statements differ from specific ones: Scientists revise models; the scientists who conducted this study revised the model. Avoid deleting an article merely because Hindi has no matching article system.
examples: The evidence is persuasive, but it is not conclusive.
A particular body of evidence supports a view without proving it decisively.
Evidence is uncountable; persuasive and conclusive express different strengths.
She has considerable experience, but this was an unusual experience.
She has substantial accumulated knowledge; this event was unusual.
The same noun changes countability with meaning.
exercises: Correct: The researcher collected many evidences and gave an useful explanation.
The researcher collected substantial evidence and gave a useful explanation. Evidence is normally uncountable; useful begins with a consonant sound /j/.
Explain the difference between a solution and the solution.
A solution introduces one possible answer. The solution identifies a contextually known or uniquely relevant answer; it does not automatically mean the only imaginable solution.

sections.title: Time, aspect and narrative perspective
sections.explanation:
Tense and aspect are not interchangeable. The simple form can present a fact or event as a whole; the progressive presents an activity from inside its unfolding; the perfect relates an earlier situation to a reference time. I have worked here for years connects earlier work with the present. I worked there for years places it in a finished past frame. I had worked there for years makes a later past moment the reference point.
Stative verbs often resist a progressive in their ordinary meanings, but meanings can change: I think it is correct expresses an opinion; I am thinking about it describes an active process. Do not add a perfect merely to sound advanced. Use past simple with a finished past-time expression: I submitted it yesterday. In a narrative, establish the time frame clearly and use past perfect only where the earlier relationship needs marking.
examples: By the time the review began, we had already revised the report.
The revision preceded the beginning of the review.
Past perfect anchors one past event before another.
I have been reading the report, but I have not finished it.
Reading has occupied the recent period; completion has not occurred.
Perfect progressive emphasises the activity, while the perfect marks the result.
exercises: Explain: I have lived here for five years / I lived here for five years.
The first ordinarily includes the present. The second describes a finished period, though fuller context can refine that interpretation.
Correct: I have met her last Tuesday.
I met her last Tuesday. A finished, explicitly dated past event normally takes past simple.

sections.title: Modality, inference and counterfactuals
sections.explanation:
Modal verbs express different kinds of meaning: permission, obligation, ability, probability or inference. Must in You must submit the form is an obligation; must in She must have left is an inference. Must not is prohibition, while do not have to is absence of necessity. Could have can describe an unrealised possibility or an uncertain explanation; context decides.
Use counterfactual conditionals to control the relationship between condition and consequence. If we had checked, we would have noticed refers to an unrealised past. If I had accepted that job, I would live abroad now combines a past condition with a present consequence. Do not mechanically use would in every if-clause. Hedging is not vagueness: may, is likely to and must have commit to different strengths.
examples: The result may reflect a sampling bias.
Sampling bias is a possible explanation.
May marks possibility, not a demonstrated cause.
If the records had been complete, we would know the answer now.
Past incompleteness explains present uncertainty.
Mixed conditional: past condition, present result.
exercises: Distinguish must not enter from do not have to enter.
Must not enter forbids entry. Do not have to enter allows staying out but does not forbid entering.
Make a cautious inference from an unanswered email without claiming certainty.
She may not have seen the message yet. This preserves alternative explanations.

sections.title: Information structure, inversion and emphasis
sections.explanation:
A grammatical sentence can still present information awkwardly. Place familiar information where it helps the reader connect to the preceding sentence, and reserve the end for a useful new focus. A cleft such as What matters is the quality of the evidence highlights one component. It was the second trial that failed contrasts that trial with others.
Negative or restrictive fronting can trigger subject-auxiliary inversion: Rarely do we see this pattern; Only after the review did we identify the error. If there is no auxiliary, introduce do in an appropriate tense. Not every initial adverb triggers inversion. Under no circumstances and not until are strong rhetorical choices; repeated inversion can sound theatrical in ordinary correspondence.
examples: Only after the second review did we identify the omission.
The omission was identified after, not before, that review.
Fronted restrictive phrase triggers did + subject + base verb.
What the analysis establishes is a correlation.
Correlation is the focused result.
A wh-cleft controls emphasis and does not strengthen correlation into causation.
exercises: Rewrite with fronted Never: I have never encountered this problem.
Never have I encountered this problem. The auxiliary precedes the subject.
Why is Only the supervisor approved it different?
Only modifies the subject itself, so it does not trigger subject-auxiliary inversion.

sections.title: Academic precision, evidence and synthesis
sections.explanation:
Distinguish reporting from endorsement. The author argues that introduces a position; the results indicate that presents evidence; it has been established that asserts a stronger consensus. Qualify scope explicitly: in this sample, under these conditions, over the study period. Statistical significance is not the same as practical importance.
Summarise the reasoning, not a sequence of disconnected quotations. A synthesis states how sources relate: agreement on observations but disagreement on mechanism; similar conclusions reached by different methods; or differences caused by population and measurement. Avoid nominalisations that hide agents or responsibility. The implementation of a revision occurred is usually less useful than The team revised the protocol.
examples: Although the findings are consistent with the hypothesis, they do not rule out alternative explanations.
The evidence fits the hypothesis but does not establish exclusivity.
Concession plus a limit on inference.
The two accounts agree on the outcome but differ in their explanation of its cause.
Their observations converge; their causal interpretations do not.
Parallel structure makes the comparison precise.
exercises: We found an association. Rewrite without claiming causation.
The study found an association between the variables; the design does not establish that one caused the other.
Replace: The execution of the assessment was undertaken by the panel.
The panel conducted the assessment. A clear agent and verb improve readability.

sections.title: Register, diplomacy and professional control
sections.explanation:
Professional politeness combines clarity with proportionate consideration. A request can use Could you, Would you be able to or I would appreciate, but piling them together sounds cumbersome. Explain the practical reason and propose a next step. Tactful disagreement should identify the precise point: I agree with the overall aim; my concern is the assumption about cost.
Register depends on audience, medium and relationship. Contractions can be natural in many professional emails. Legal and technical contexts may require precise conventional language. Avoid importing casual idioms into a formal report, and avoid bureaucratic language in a message to a friend. A firm refusal can be courteous without becoming ambiguous.
examples: Could you confirm whether the revised deadline is feasible?
Please assess the new deadline and reply.
Whether introduces alternatives; feasible concerns practicality.
I can support the proposal provided that the budget assumptions are clarified.
Support is conditional on clarification.
Provided that expresses a real condition politely.
exercises: Rewrite politely and clearly: You did not explain this. Send it now.
Could you clarify how this figure was calculated? We need the explanation before completing the review.
Write a firm refusal with an alternative.
We cannot complete the full review by Friday. We can deliver the priority findings then and the remaining analysis on Tuesday. The refusal stays explicit.

sections.title: Editing for style, rhythm and naturalness
sections.explanation:
Check collocation before choosing a sophisticated synonym: make a decision, reach a conclusion, pose a question, conduct research. Words can share a dictionary gloss yet differ in typical partners. Strong prose varies sentence length according to purpose. Use parallel syntax for parallel ideas and a short sentence for a decisive implication.
Ambiguous pronouns, dangling modifiers and misplaced negation can change meaning. After reviewing the evidence, the conclusion became clear incorrectly assigns the review to the conclusion. Repair the agent: After reviewing the evidence, we reached a clearer conclusion. Only can attach to different parts of a sentence; place it near its intended focus. Naturalness comes from contemporary examples, not a list of ornamental idioms.
examples: The policy is simple to explain, difficult to implement and expensive to maintain.
Three comparable properties are listed.
Parallel adjective + infinitive pattern creates coherence.
We reviewed only the first report.
The review was restricted to that report.
Only scopes the object rather than the identity of the reviewers.
exercises: Correct the dangling modifier: Walking into the room, the results were surprising.
When I walked into the room, I was surprised by the results. The person doing the walking is explicit.
Improve: We did a conclusion after making research.
We reached a conclusion after conducting research. Collocations and uncountable research are repaired.

sections.title: UK and US accents: choosing reference models
sections.explanation:
Accent is pronunciation; dialect also includes grammar and vocabulary. The UK includes London, northern English, Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish varieties, among many others. The US includes regional and social varieties beyond General American. The two reference models here are useful learning anchors, not national uniformity.
A major distinction is rhoticity. Most General American speech pronounces /r/ after a vowel in car and hard. Many southern British varieties do not pronounce that /r/ before a consonant or pause, but may link it before a following vowel: far away. Scottish and some other UK varieties are rhotic. In General American, /r/ can be bunched or retroflex; do not replace it with a Hindi tap or trill when practising that model.
Record the same paragraph in your chosen reference model. First compare /r/, then vowels, then rhythm. Preserve intelligibility before pursuing subtle regional features.
examples: car: reference UK /kɑː/; reference US /kɑr/
The US model retains post-vocalic /r/.
The vowel quality and exact /r/ vary by speaker.
far away: UK linking /r/ may occur before the vowel of away.
A non-rhotic speaker can pronounce /r/ at a word boundary before a vowel.
Non-rhotic does not mean deleting every written r.
exercises: Which words expose rhoticity: red, hard, very, teacher?
Hard and teacher before a pause expose post-vocalic /r/. Red and very have /r/ before a vowel in both reference models.
Should Scottish speech be described as non-rhotic UK English?
No. Many Scottish varieties are rhotic; national labels are too broad.

sections.title: UK and US vowels and consonants
sections.explanation:
Learn contrasts through sound, not spelling. A common southern British distinction in the BATH set gives bath and dance /ɑː/, while General American commonly uses /æ/. Many northern English accents also use a short /a/-type vowel in these words. Reference British hot has /ɒ/; General American typically has an /ɑ/-type vowel. The LOT/THOUGHT merger varies across US speakers.
In many American accents, /t/ and /d/ can become a flap [ɾ] between appropriate vowel sounds when the following syllable is unstressed, as in writer and ladder. This is not the rule that every t becomes d. British /t/ can be clearly released, unreleased or glottalised depending on context and speaker. General American often has a more widespread dark /l/; both reference models can have dark /l/ in final positions. Practise contrasts with a recording rather than exaggerating a national stereotype.
examples: bath: reference UK /bɑːθ/; reference US /bæθ/
The reference vowels differ; both end with /θ/.
This distinction does not describe every British accent.
writer can contain a flap [ɾ] in General American.
The medial consonant may resemble a brief tap.
It is context-dependent and should not be replaced mechanically with a full /d/.
exercises: Practise thin /θɪn/ and then /ðen/. What changes?
The tongue is near the teeth in both. /θ/ is voiceless and /ð/ voiced. Avoid consistently substituting /t/, /d/ or /s/ if the distinction affects clarity.
Why is a single rule for US hot and caught unreliable?
Some American speakers merge their vowels and others distinguish them. Select a real model speaker and follow that system consistently.

sections.title: Connected speech, stress, rhythm and intonation
sections.explanation:
English speech groups words into meaning units. Content words often carry prominence; grammatical words often weaken, but contrast can make any word prominent. To commonly weakens to /tə/ and and to /ən/ in suitable unstressed contexts. These reductions belong to speech; do not write gonna in a formal report merely because you hear it.
The location of sentence stress can change the implied correction: I wanted the BLUE one contrasts colour; I WANTED the blue one contrasts intention with some other relation. Use pauses to clarify clause boundaries and reserve the main pitch movement for the intended focus. English is often described as stress-timed, but do not force mechanically equal intervals between stressed syllables. Natural timing varies with speaker and situation.
For practice, mark thought groups with a vertical bar, underline prominent words and record. Compare whether listeners hear the intended contrast, not just whether the recording sounds fast.
examples: I said she could BORROW it, not keep it.
Borrowing rather than ownership is the contrast.
The prominence carries the correction.
Although the sample was small | the pattern was consistent.
A concession is followed by the main observation.
A thought-group boundary supports interpretation.
exercises: Say: I did not say he stole it. Move stress to I, say, he and stole.
Each placement suggests a different correction: speaker, wording, person or action. Explain the intended implication before recording.
Make a 30-second accent practice log.
Record the model, your attempt and one measurable focus, such as maintaining /θ/ in three words. Do not rate yourself solely on speed.

sections.title: Regional vocabulary, spelling and advanced reading
sections.explanation:
UK/US distinctions include colour/color, centre/center, pavement/sidewalk and flat/apartment. Usage overlaps and terminology depends on context: first floor is above the ground floor in typical British building numbering, but commonly ground level in US numbering. Check the actual location. Collective agreement also varies: British the team are can emphasise members; American the team is is more usual as a default. Both systems allow contextual choices.
Original teaching passage: A public debate can become polarised even when participants agree on the observations. They may disagree about which risks deserve priority, or about who should bear the cost of reducing them. A careful reader therefore separates empirical disagreement from disagreement over values. Recognising that distinction does not settle the debate, but it makes the reasoning easier to evaluate.
The passage uses concession, modal possibility, embedded questions and a limited conclusion. Notice that may avoids asserting a universal explanation. Read it aloud in your chosen reference accent without changing its formal register.
examples: Participants may disagree about who should bear the cost.
The disagreement can concern responsibility for cost.
The embedded question keeps declarative word order.
Recognising the distinction does not settle the debate.
Analysis improves clarity without guaranteeing agreement.
The gerund clause serves as subject; negation limits the claim.
exercises: Summarise the passage in 40 words.
Debates may reflect differences in values and risk priorities rather than observations. Separating these forms of disagreement helps evaluate reasoning, although it does not itself produce agreement.
Write two professional versions of an email, one with consistent UK spelling and one with US spelling.
Check consistency, terminology and audience expectations. Neither version should become a caricature of national speech.

rules.title: Articles, countability and reference
rules.explanation: Article choice reflects reference and countability. A/an selects a singular countable noun and follows the initial sound, not the first letter. Research and evidence are normally uncountable in academic uses; experience can change countability with meaning.

examples.native: This is the opposite of what I expected.
examples.translation: मुझे जो अपेक्षा थी उसके यह विपरीत है।

examples.native: My grandfather was murdered during the Second World War.
examples.translation: दूसरे विश्वयुद्ध के दौरान मेरे दादा का खून हुआ था।

examples.native: He entered the room slowly by that door.
examples.translation: वह उस दरवाज़े से धीरे से कमरे में घुसा।

rules.title: Perfect auxiliaries and reference time
rules.explanation: A perfect relates an earlier situation to a reference time. Have/has normally anchors the present; had anchors a past reference point. The auxiliary can also be ordinary possession, so inspect the participle and time phrase.

examples.native: Please give me the paper when you have done with it.
examples.translation: जब आपने अखबार पढ़ लिया हो तो मुझे दे दीजिएगा।

examples.native: His health has enabled him to succeed in life.
examples.translation: उसके स्वास्थ्य ने उसको ज़िन्दगी में कामयाब होने दिया है।

examples.native: My pen has run out of ink! Can I borrow your pen?
examples.translation: मेरी कलम में स्याही खतम हो गई है। मैं तुम्हारी कलम ले सकता हूँ क्या?

rules.title: Progressive perspective
rules.explanation: A progressive presents a situation from within its unfolding. Stative versus dynamic interpretations matter. The -ing form also serves in non-finite clauses and noun-like uses, so an -ing word alone does not prove a progressive.

examples.native: One of the lights is not working. Do you think you could come take a look?
examples.translation: एक बत्ती नहीं जल रही है। तुम ज़रा आकर देख सकते हो क्या?

examples.native: Are these the glasses you were looking for?
examples.translation: क्या यह वह ऐनक है जिसे आप ढूँढ रहे थे ?

examples.native: The scientists are working on a new experiment.
examples.translation: वैज्ञानिक नए प्रयोग पर काम कर रहे है I

rules.title: Modal inference
rules.explanation: Modal meaning depends on context: inference, permission, ability and obligation differ. Must have + participle commonly makes a past inference; might have leaves alternatives open. Absence of necessity is not prohibition.

examples.native: In order to stay awake I may have to drink more coffee.
examples.translation: मुझे जगे रहने के लिए शायद और कॉफ़ी पीनी पड़ेगी।

examples.native: I was scared that you might leave me.
examples.translation: मुझे डर था कि तुम मुझे छोड़ दोगे।

examples.native: Oh, I do wish I could go to France.
examples.translation: ओह, काश मैं फ़्रान्स जा सकती!

rules.title: Past modal constructions
rules.pattern: \b(?:should have|could have|would have|must have|might have|may have)\b
rules.explanation: Modal + have + participle relates modality to a prior event. Could have can mean unrealised opportunity or uncertain explanation. Match the speaker’s commitment and the intended timeline.

examples.native: Something must have happened to him on the way.
examples.translation: उसके साथ रास्ते पर कुछ हुआ होगा।

examples.native: If I had known her address, I would have written to her.
examples.translation: अगर मुझे उसका पता पता होता, तो मैंने उसे चिट्ठी लिखी हुई होती।

examples.native: With a little more patience, you would have succeeded.
examples.translation: अगर तुममें थोड़ा और सब्र होता तो तुम कामयाब हो जाते।

rules.title: Conditional relationships
rules.explanation: Choose tense and modal forms according to reality and temporal relation. If + past perfect can describe an unreal past condition; a present consequence creates a mixed conditional. Unless is not a free substitute for every if not.

examples.native: Keep hold of my hand if you're afraid.
examples.translation: मेरा हाथ पकड़लो अगर तुम्हे डर लग रहा है तो।

examples.native: Tom wouldn't be here if it wasn't for me.
examples.translation: मैं ना होता तो टॉम आज यहाँ नहीं होता।

examples.native: You will get fat if you eat too much.
examples.translation: बहुत ज़्यादा खा लिया तो मोटे हो जाओगे।

rules.title: Negative and restrictive emphasis
rules.explanation: Fronted negative/restrictive adverbials can trigger subject–auxiliary inversion. Only before the subject does not: Only Anna agreed. Scope and placement decide what the restriction actually excludes.

examples.native: The capital of Himachal Pradesh, Shimla, is only 115 kilometres away from Chandigarh.
examples.translation: हिमाचल प्रदेश की राजधानी, शिमला, चण्डीगढ़ से केवल ११५ किलोमीटर की दूरी पर है।

examples.native: No matter what happens, I will never betray my friend.
examples.translation: चाहे जो भी हो, मैं कभी भी अपने दोस्त को धोखा नहीं दूँगा।

examples.native: He'll never admit to being in the wrong.
examples.translation: वह कभी अपनी ग़लती नहीं मानेगा।

rules.title: Cleft and focus structures
rules.explanation: Clefts and related constructions organise focus: What matters is accuracy. A form such as what can also introduce a question or relative structure, so identify what the sentence highlights and its grammatical frame.

examples.native: It was the window that Tom broke yesterday.
examples.translation: वह वह खिड़की है जिसको टॉम ने कल थोड़ा था।

examples.native: What were you and Tom doing in the attic?
examples.translation: तुम और टौम पडछत्ती पर क्या कर रहे थे?

examples.native: What he did was nothing less than madness.
examples.translation: उसने जो किया वह पागलपन से कुछ कम नहीं था।

rules.title: Relative clauses
rules.explanation: Relative forms connect an antecedent to a clause. Restrictive and supplementary clauses differ in punctuation and meaning. Whose expresses a possessive relation; whom is an object form mainly retained in formal contexts.

examples.native: The passengers who were injured in the accident were taken to the nearest hospital.
examples.translation: जिन यात्रियों को दुर्घटना मे चोट आई थी उन्हे अस्पताल ले जाया गया।

examples.native: Mother Teresa was a Catholic nun who lived and worked in Calcutta, India.
examples.translation: मदर टेरेसा एक कैथोलिक नन थीं जो कलकत्ता में रहतीं और काम करतीं थीं।

examples.native: I know a girl who can ride a unicycle.
examples.translation: मेरे जान-पहचान की एक लड़की को युनिसायकल चलाना आता है।

rules.title: Embedded questions
rules.explanation: Embedded questions ordinarily have statement order: I wonder where she is. Whether can introduce explicit alternatives. Do not carry direct-question inversion into an ordinary embedded question.

examples.native: I don't know how to operate this computer.
examples.translation: मुझे यह कम्प्यूटर चलाना नहीं आता।

examples.native: She's trying to whistle, but she doesn't know how.
examples.translation: वह सीटी बजाने की कोशिश कर रही है, मगर उसे बजाने नहीं आती।

examples.native: Tom wants to know why you didn't call him back.
examples.translation: टॉम पूछ रहा है कि तुमने उसे कॉल बैक क्यों नहीं किया।

rules.title: Concession and limits on claims
rules.explanation: Although introduces a finite concessive clause; despite usually takes a noun phrase or -ing construction. However/nevertheless link discourse differently. A concessive sentence can accept evidence while limiting the conclusion.

examples.native: Although fatalities tend to be rare, many people died as a result of volcanic eruptions during the last quarter century.
examples.translation: घायलो की संख्या कम है पर पिछले सवा सौ वर्षों में ज्वालामुखी विस्फोटो के कारण बहुत लोग मरे है ।

examples.native: Though he is rich, he is not happy.
examples.translation: वह अमीर हो कर भी ख़ुश नहीं है।

examples.native: It is, however, apposite to note that this process will continue in the year ahead.
examples.translation: तथापि, यह नोट करना उपयुक्त है कि यह प्रक्रिया अगले वर्ष जारी रहेगी।

rules.title: Cause, purpose and consequence
rules.explanation: Distinguish a reason, a purpose and an outcome. Since can be temporal or causal. Therefore signals a supported consequence; it does not itself prove a causal mechanism.

examples.native: I love life because what more is there.
examples.translation: मैं जीवन से प्यार करता हूँ क्योंकि और है ही क्या।

examples.native: Because of his advice, I was able to succeed.
examples.translation: मैं उसकी सलाह की वजह से कामयाब हो गया।

examples.native: Because of the rain they had to cancel the game.
examples.translation: बारिश की वजह से उन्हें खेल रद्द करना पड़ा।

rules.title: Passive and agency
rules.explanation: A be form plus a past participle can build a passive; a be form alone can be a copula/progressive auxiliary. Passive voice helps manage focus but can also hide an agent. Restore the agent when responsibility matters.

examples.native: These texts were written in Hebrew, not in Aramaic.
examples.translation: यह पाठ्य इब्रानी में लिखे थे, आरामाईक में नहीं।

examples.native: Their conversation was carried on for about an hour.
examples.translation: उनकी बातचीत लगभग एक घंटे तक चलती रही।

examples.native: Sam joined the army when he was eighteen.
examples.translation: सैम अठारह साल की उम्र में आर्मी में भर्ती हुआ था।

rules.title: Non-finite complements
rules.explanation: Complement patterns belong to the governing word: decide to act, avoid acting, insist on acting. To can be infinitive marker or preposition. Do not assume a synonym accepts the same complement pattern.

examples.native: Traveling by boat takes longer than going by car.

examples.native: Goals determine what you are going to be.

examples.native: This is Tom speaking. I'd like to speak to Ann.
examples.translation: मैं टॉम बोल रहा हूँ। मुझे ऐन से बात करनी है।

rules.title: Pronoun reference and reflexives
rules.explanation: A reflexive typically refers back to an appropriate antecedent. It can also add emphasis. Professional style does not require replacing me with myself when no reflexive relation exists.

examples.native: Maybe I am unhappy, but I don't intend to kill myself.
examples.translation: हाँ शायद मैं दुखी हूँ, पर मुझे अपनी जान लेने का इरादा नहीं है।

examples.native: When you betray somebody else, you also betray yourself.
examples.translation: आप किसी व्यक्ति को धोखा देते हैं तो आप अपने आप को भी धोखा देते हैं।

examples.native: You need to be attentive during the interview and grab any opportunity that presents itself.
examples.translation: इंटरव्यू के दौरान तुम्हें सतर्क रहना होगा और मौक़ा दिखते ही उसे हाथ ले लेना होगा।

rules.title: Quantifiers and agreement
rules.explanation: Quantifiers interact with countability and agreement. Much/little often pair with uncountables, many/few with count plurals. Each/every usually selects singular agreement, while usage around either/neither can depend on the full construction.

rules.title: Time-frame control
rules.explanation: Time expressions help establish an interval/reference point but do not select a tense mechanically. Ago normally locates a finished past time. Since marks a starting point; for a duration in relevant uses.

examples.native: That was just the trailer, the movie's yet to come, my friend!

rules.title: Comparison and parallel structure
rules.explanation: A comparison needs a clear standard and comparable structures. As ... as expresses equality; more/less ... than inequality. Ellipsis can omit understood material but should not create ambiguity.

rules.title: Reported speech and stance
rules.explanation: Reporting verbs encode stance and govern distinct complements. Say and tell differ in object requirements; suggest does not accept every pattern that advise accepts. Reporting a claim is not endorsing it.

rules.title: Hedging and professional modality
rules.explanation: Hedges express different strengths and types of commitment. Could you is often a request, not a question about physical ability. Pair a precise request with a practical reason; avoid stacking several courtesy formulas.

passages.title: History: evidence and perspective
passages.native: Two accounts of the same event need not differ because one author is dishonest. Each may have had access to different evidence, written for a different audience or considered a different question important. A historian compares sources before choosing an interpretation. The date of a document, its intended reader and the circumstances of its production help establish what it can reveal. Silence is also difficult to interpret: the absence of a statement is not necessarily evidence that an event never occurred. A careful account distinguishes what is directly documented from what is inferred.
passages.guide: Identify how the writer distinguishes evidence, interpretation and uncertainty. Summarise the reasoning in your own words.

grammarTerms: Noun
A word naming a person, thing or idea: student, book, freedom.
Verb
A word describing an action or state: read, know, be.
Subject
The participant linked to the main verb’s subject pattern. In The student reads a book, the student is the subject.
Object
A participant selected by a verb. In The student reads a book, a book is the direct object.
Agreement
One word changes to match another, for example an adjective matching a noun’s gender and number.
Case
A noun/pronoun form marking its relationship in a sentence. Cases can mark subjects, objects, possession or relations usually expressed by English prepositions.
Gender
A grammatical noun class. It does not always describe the sex of a person or any physical property.
Tense
A verb system that relates a situation to a time, often past or non-past.
Aspect
How a situation is viewed: unfolding, completed, habitual, experienced or in a resulting state.
Infinitive
A non-finite verb form often used for a dictionary entry or a complement. It does not by itself give the ordinary person/tense pattern.
Participle
A verb-derived form used in compound predicates or as a modifier; its exact function depends on the language and construction.
Clause
A unit organised around a predicate. One sentence can contain several clauses.
Register
Language choices suited to a situation: casual conversation, polite requests, academic writing or another context.
